extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (introductory discrete mathematics / symbolic logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Translating English mathematical sentences into symbolic logic and manipulating logical statements (truth tables, equivalence, negation, quantifiers) for use in proofs and problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation precedence and use of parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbol ~ negates the expression it precedes. Thus ~PvQ means (~P)vQ, not ~(PvQ). In ~ (P v Q), the value of the entire expression P v Q is negated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with placement of parentheses; ~ binds to the immediate expression that follows unless parentheses group a larger expression. Examples in text: ~PvQ = (~P)vQ, whereas ~(PvQ) negates the whole disjunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a conditional's truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "If P, then Q" is a statement. This statement is true if it's impossible for P to be true while Q is false; it is false if there is at least one instance in which P is true but Q is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition when judging truth of implications (including quantified implications). Example: a multiple-of-6 implies even is true for all integers; even implies multiple-of-6 is not true for all integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit universal quantifier for unquantified conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, whenever P(x) and Q(x) are open sentences about elements x in some set S, an expression of the form P(x) => Q(x) is understood to be the statement ∀x ∈ S, P(x) => Q(x) if not explicitly quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention avoids repeatedly writing ∀x. Be mindful that without an explicit quantifier an expression with variables is treated as universally quantified (i.e., becomes a statement with definite truth value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier meanings (universal and existential)
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbol ∀ stands for 'for all' (universal quantifier) and ∃ stands for 'there exists' (existential quantifier). ∀x∈S, P(x) is true iff P(x) is true for every x∈S. ∃x∈S, P(x) is true iff P(x) is true for at least one x∈S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate English quantifier phrases carefully into ∀ and ∃ forms. Examples: 'For every real x there is a real y with y^2 = x' → ∀x∈R ∃y∈R, y^2 = x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negate quantifiers by switching ∀↔∃ and negating the predicate; with multiple quantifiers apply these rules iteratively. Example demonstrated: negation of ∀x ∃y, y^3 = x becomes ∃x ∀y, y^3 ≠ x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifiers matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement contains two (or more) quantifiers, reversing their order can change the meaning and truth value of the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∀x ∃y, y^2 = x is true (every real has a square root in reals with sign choices), but ∃y ∀x, y^2 = x is false. Always maintain intended quantifier order when translating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't mechanically replace English 'and'/'or'
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating English to symbolic logic, do not automatically replace every 'and' with ∧ and every 'or' with ∨; attend to intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At least one of the integers x and y is even' should be (x is even) ∨ (y is even), not (x is even) ∧ (y is even). The logical meaning of 'but' is captured by 'and'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of logical equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth values match up line-for-line in a truth table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical equivalence allows replacing one expression by another in proofs or simplifications. Verify non-obvious equivalences with truth tables; examples in text include P↔Q = (P∧Q)∨(~P∧~Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use truth tables to verify equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: To see if two propositional expressions are equivalent, write truth tables for them (putting both expressions into the same table is efficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include helper columns for intermediate expressions (e.g., ~P, ~Q, P∧Q, ~P∧~Q). The example shows P↔Q and (P∧Q)∨(~P∧~Q) placed in same table to verify equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: P↔Q is true exactly when P and Q are both true or both false; equivalently P↔Q = (P∧Q) ∨ (~P∧~Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form to reason about equality of truth values or to transform biconditionals into conjunctions/disjunctions for truth-table checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's laws
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are essential transformation rules used to negate compound statements; the text verifies the first with a truth table and leaves the second as an exercise. Apply them when negating disjunctions/conjunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A conditional P => Q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive (~Q => ~P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is useful in proofs: sometimes proving (~Q => ~P) is easier than proving (P => Q). The text suggests rewriting implications in contrapositive form when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutative, distributive, and associative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Commutative: P∧Q = Q∧P, P∨Q = Q∨P. Distributive: P∧(Q∨R) = (P∧Q)∨(P∧R), P∨(Q∧R) = (P∨Q)∧(P∨R). Associative: P∧(Q∧R) = (P∧Q)∧R (and similarly for ∨).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These algebra-like laws let you rearrange and regroup logical expressions; associative laws justify dropping parentheses when only one operator type appears in a chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses when mixing ∧ and ∨
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses are essential when there is a mix of ∧ and ∨ (e.g., P ∨ (Q ∧ R) is not logically equivalent to (P ∨ Q) ∧ R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not drop parentheses if both conjunction and disjunction appear; exercise in text warns that the two forms are not equivalent and points to an exercise to check this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating a conditional
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this identity when you need to express that an implication is false (there exists a case where P true and Q false). The text uses truth-table reasoning to justify this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating complex statements via DeMorgan and quantifier rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When negating complex or multi-quantifier statements, apply DeMorgan's laws and quantifier-negation rules iteratively to derive an equivalent (often simpler) negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: negating ∀x ∃y, y^3 = x leads to ∃x ∀y, y^3 ≠ x by successive application of ~(∀...) = ∃~(...) and ~(P=>Q)=P∧~Q where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentence vs statement distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: An open sentence contains variables whose truth depends on variable values; a statement has a definite truth value. Adding a universal quantifier ∀ in front of an implication P(x)=>Q(x) turns it into a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful when translating: an unquantified conditional with variables describes an open sentence and only becomes a statement when quantified (often implicitly by convention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical inference rules (basic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several inference patterns are fundamental: Modus Ponens (from P=>Q and P infer Q); if P and Q are true then P∧Q is true; from P∧Q infer P (and infer Q); from P infer P∨Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also use disjunctive syllogism: from P∨Q and ~Q infer P. These are patterns to produce new valid statements from known true statements; verify via truth tables if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication principle for counting lists
rubrics_metrics.description: If making a list of length n there are a1 choices for first entry, a2 for second, ..., an for nth entry, then the total number of different lists is a1 * a2 * ... * an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tree/branching reasoning to visualize choices; example: three-letter-then-four-digit license plates give 26*26*26*10*10*10*10 possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists: order, repetition, notation, and empty list
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence (parentheses with comma-separated entries); order matters and repeats are allowed. Two lists are equal only if they have identical entries in identical order. The empty list () has length zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer parentheses/comma notation to avoid ambiguity (e.g., (9,10,11) should not be conflated with concatenated digits). Length equals number of entries; unequal lengths imply lists are not equal.
